questions.q: A dummy model that predicts 'stayed' for everyone scores 0.889 accuracy on the capstone data. What does this tell you?
options: The problem is easy to solve
Accuracy is misleading here because only about 11% of customers cancel
questions.explain: With an 11% positive rate, predicting the majority class already gives high accuracy while catching no cancellers. That is why the capstone uses average precision and ROC AUC.

questions.q: Why write the success criteria before building any model?
options: It makes the models train faster
It stops you from moving the goalposts after you see the results
It removes the need for a test set
questions.explain: Fixing the metric, validation plan, and cost target in advance keeps the evaluation honest instead of tuned to flatter the model.

questions.q: What does average precision equal for a model that ranks customers at random, and what was it here?
options: The positive rate of the data, 0.111
The accuracy of the dummy model, 0.889
questions.explain: A random ranking has precision equal to the base rate at every recall level, so its average precision is about the cancel rate. ROC AUC for random is 0.5.

questions.q: In the lesson's illustrative costs, an offer costs 10 and a missed cancellation costs 100. Why does 'contact everybody' (10,000 per 1,000 customers) beat 'contact nobody' (about 11,125)?
options: Cancellations are expensive relative to offers, and about 11% of customers cancel
Contacting everybody has no false positives
questions.explain: Nobody-cost is 1,000 x 0.111 x 100, roughly 11,125. Everybody-cost is 1,000 x 10 = 10,000. A model must beat the cheaper of the two.

questions.q: Why is the test set split off with stratify=y and then left untouched during exploration and tuning?
options: Stratifying makes the model more accurate
The test set is too small for training
It keeps the class balance equal in both parts, and protects the final estimate from leakage
It lets you tune the threshold on it
questions.explain: Stratification keeps the 11% cancel rate in both sets. Keeping the test set sealed means it gives one honest estimate at the end.
